There’s a quiet, undeniable magic in the concept of *deep time*. When we walk through a dense forest, we witness a mere snapshot of a single fleeting afternoon. Yet, beneath the crunchy layers of fallen leaves and moss, lies an unimaginable, sprawling saga. Deep time is the realization that the ground we casually tread upon was once the floor of a vast, ancient ocean or the towering peak of a jagged mountain range that has since been whittled to dust by the wind.

Think of a smooth river stone. To us, it is merely a small, pocket-sized object, cool to the touch and entirely unremarkable. But to the Earth, it is the indestructible ghost of a billion forgotten years. It holds the memory of violent volcanic eruptions, the slow, creeping freeze of massive ice ages, and the silent weight of mile-deep glaciers. 

We measure our fleeting lives in heartbeats and coffee breaks, distressed by a late train or a misplaced set of keys. But if you sit quietly on a piece of exposed bedrock and press your palm flat against its rough surface, you can almost feel the planet’s slow, heavy breathing. We are merely passing shadows, flashes of brilliant lightning across the immense, dark sky of geological history. There is immense comfort in that insignificance. Our mistakes are temporary, our grief will erode like soft clay, and our joy is a sudden, beautiful spark in the endless, quiet night. We are the universe briefly waking up to marvel at itself.
